statement: Three vertices of a parallelogram are $(1, 1)$, $(4, 2)$ and $(2, 5)$. The fourth vertex could be at more than one point. Over all possible locations $(x, y)$ of the fourth vertex, what is the greatest possible value of $x + y$?

choices.misconception: I only built the parallelogram with (2, 5) opposite the new vertex, which gives (3, -2), and missed the other two possibilities.
I assumed the vertices go around the parallelogram in the order given, which gives only (-1, 4), and missed the other two possibilities.
I added the first two points, (1, 1) + (4, 2) = (5, 3), and forgot to subtract the third point.
I added up all six coordinates of the three given points.

hints: In a parallelogram the two diagonals have the same midpoint, so the two pairs of opposite vertices add up to the same point, adding $x$ to $x$ and $y$ to $y$.
Any one of the three given points can be the vertex opposite the missing one. That gives three cases.
The missing vertex is the sum of two given points minus the third: $(3, -2)$, $(-1, 4)$ or $(5, 6)$.

solutions.reliable: Opposite vertices of a parallelogram share a midpoint, so if $V$ is opposite a given point $Z$ and the other two given points are $X$ and $Y$, then $V + Z = X + Y$ and $V = X + Y - Z$. With $(2, 5)$ opposite: $V = (1, 1) + (4, 2) - (2, 5) = (3, -2)$, so $x + y = 1$. With $(4, 2)$ opposite: $V = (1, 1) + (2, 5) - (4, 2) = (-1, 4)$, so $x + y = 3$. With $(1, 1)$ opposite: $V = (4, 2) + (2, 5) - (1, 1) = (5, 6)$, so $x + y = 11$. None of these four-point sets has three points on a line, so all three are real parallelograms, and the greatest value is $11$.
solutions.elegant: Work only with the sums $x + y$: the given points have sums $2$, $6$ and $7$, and the missing vertex has sum (one of them) $+$ (another) $-$ (the third). To make it largest, subtract the smallest: $6 + 7 - 2 = 11$.
